\chapter{Friend and Family}
\label{ch:mr-friend-and-family}
\hlchaptermodality{12}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a friend, a family, a brother, and a sister in Marathi, sort each word into a tatsama taken up whole from Sanskrit or a tadbhava worn down by sound change, and say which sibling word is genuinely English's cousin and which is not.}

The chapter closes on \mr{बहीण}, deliberately not a cousin of English sister: the reader produces \mr{मित्र}, \mr{कुटुंब}, \mr{भाऊ} and \mr{बहीण}, sorts the four into two tatsamas (\mr{मित्र}, \mr{कुटुंब}) and two tadbhavas (\mr{भाऊ}, \mr{बहीण}), and names \mr{भाऊ} as the secure cousin of brother against \mr{बहीण}'s unrelated root — while recalling \mr{कुटुंब}'s gender split from Hindi and \mr{मित्र}'s root in a covenant god's name.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mitra]{\mr{मित्र} (mitra) — a friend, and a very old bond}

\label{lesson:MR-C11-mitra}



\begin{quote}
You can ask for \textbf{bhākarī} now. This chapter turns from what you'd request to who you'd share it with.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{मित्र}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मित्र}} — \emph{mitra} — \textbf{friend} (masculine)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Two things worth pausing on. \textbf{\mr{ि}}, the \textbf{short \emph{i}} vowel sign, is new — written \emph{before} the consonant it belongs to but said \emph{after} it, so \textbf{\mr{मि}} is read \emph{mi}, not \emph{im}. And \textbf{\mr{त्र}} is \textbf{\mr{त}} joined to \textbf{\mr{र}} by a \emph{halant}, the same conjunct mechanism as \emph{punhā}'s \textbf{\mr{न्हा}}, just a different pair of letters. \emph{Mi-tra}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{मित्र}} is a \textbf{learned borrowing} straight from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{मित्र}} \emph{mitra} — taken up whole, not worn down by centuries of sound change the way most everyday words are. Its root is Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*mey-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to bind,\textquotedblright{} and the same word named a god: Avestan \textbf{Mithra} and Old Persian \textbf{Mithra} were divine witnesses to oaths — the bond itself, personified, before the word settled into ordinary Sanskrit as \textquotedblleft{}friend.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: taken up whole, not worn down}]
Sanskrit-descended Marathi words come in two kinds: a \textbf{tatsama}, borrowed directly with its Sanskrit shape mostly intact — \textbf{\mr{मित्र}} is one — and a \textbf{tadbhava}, one that passed through centuries of Prakrit sound change and came out reshaped. \textbf{\mr{भाकरी}} was neither: it never touched Sanskrit at all. This chapter will show both a tatsama and a tadbhava for family words, so you can hear the difference.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{mitra} — friend
  \item \emph{Say it:} what its root meant before \textquotedblleft{}friend\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}to bind\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Name:} the god-name that shares this root — \textbf{Mithra}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{mitra}, then \textbf{bhākarī} — a learned word beside a native one whose own root went no further back than \textquotedblleft{}a heap, a lump\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Recall:} Chapter 11's four requests and their three genders — \textbf{pāṇī} neuter, \textbf{chahā} masculine, \textbf{dūdh} neuter, \textbf{bhākarī} feminine
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \textbf{\mr{मित्र}}'s root mean before \textquotedblleft{}friend\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{To bind}.) What god-name shares that root? (\textbf{Mithra}.) Is \textbf{\mr{मित्र}} a tatsama or a tadbhava? (\textbf{Tatsama} — taken up whole from Sanskrit.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AE\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%A4\%E0\%A5\%8D\%E0\%A4\%B0}{Wiktionary: \mr{मित्र}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mitra]{One step later — retrieve \mr{मित्र}}

\label{lesson:MR-R11-mitra-r1}



\begin{quote}
Say the Marathi word for \textbf{friend} before you uncover it: \textbf{\mr{मित्र}} (\emph{mitra}).
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Its old root meant \textbf{to bind}. Marathi took the Sanskrit form up whole, so it is a \textbf{tatsama}, not a word worn down through ordinary sound change.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Answer once, then repair only the missing piece.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textbf{\mr{मित्र} — bind — tatsama.} Stop here; the next lesson adds family.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kuṭumb]{\mr{कुटुंब} (kuṭumb) — family, and a gender Hindi disagrees with}

\label{lesson:MR-C11-kutumb}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मित्र}} (\emph{mitra}) was taken up whole from Sanskrit, not worn down. This next word was too — and it names the group your friend belongs to as well.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{कुटुंब}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}} — \emph{kuṭumb} — \textbf{family} (neuter)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
One new mark: \textbf{\mr{ु}}, the \textbf{short \emph{u}} vowel sign, a small hook under the consonant — the short partner of \emph{dūdh}'s long \textbf{\mr{ू}}. \textbf{\mr{ट}} you have informally from \emph{marāṭhī}; \textbf{\mr{ं}} the familiar anusvāra. \emph{Ku-ṭu-mb}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}} is a \textbf{tatsama}, a learned borrowing from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{कुटुम्ब}} \emph{kuṭumba}, \textquotedblleft{}household, family\textquotedblright{} — like \textbf{\mr{मित्र}}, taken up whole rather than worn down by sound change. Unlike \textbf{\mr{मित्र}}, its story does not reach a secure Indo-European root: a Dravidian origin for Sanskrit's own \emph{kuṭumba} has been proposed, but it is not settled, so this lesson names the dispute rather than inventing a resolution.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a gender Hindi disagrees with}]
The very same Sanskrit word carries two different genders in its two daughters: Marathi's \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}} is \textbf{neuter}, Hindi's \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}} is \textbf{masculine}. Both borrowed the identical tatsama; each language then had to assign it a gender inside its own system, and they assigned it differently. A word's gender is not carried in with its meaning — it is decided fresh by whichever language receives it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{kuṭumb} — family
  \item \emph{State:} its gender in Marathi against Hindi — neuter here, masculine there
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{mitra}, then \textbf{kuṭumb} — two tatsamas in a row
  \item \emph{Recall:} Chapter 11's own gender lineup — \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}}'s neuter joins \textbf{\mr{पाणी}} and \textbf{\mr{दूध}}, after \textbf{bhākarī}'s feminine closed out all three genders in one chapter
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What gender is \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}} in Marathi, and how does that differ from Hindi? (\textbf{Neuter} here, \textbf{masculine} there — same borrowed word, different choice.) Is \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}}'s pre-Sanskrit origin settled? (\textbf{No} — a Dravidian source is proposed but disputed.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A5\%81\%E0\%A4\%9F\%E0\%A5\%81\%E0\%A4\%82\%E0\%A4\%AC}{Wiktionary: \mr{कुटुंब}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kutumb]{One step later — retrieve \mr{कुटुंब}}

\label{lesson:MR-R11-kutumb-r1}



\begin{quote}
Say the Marathi word for \textbf{family}: \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}} (\emph{kutumb}).
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Marathi treats \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}} as \textbf{neuter}. Hindi assigns the same borrowed word masculine gender. Retrieve the Marathi choice, not a universal rule.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Answer once, then repair only the missing piece.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textbf{\mr{कुटुंब} — family — neuter.}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhāū]{\mr{भाऊ} (bhāū) — brother, and this time the resemblance is real}

\label{lesson:MR-C11-bhau}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मित्र}} and \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}} were both taken up whole from Sanskrit. This next word was not — it was worn down, letter by letter, over centuries.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{भाऊ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{भाऊ}} — \emph{bhāū} — \textbf{brother} (masculine)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
One new letter: \textbf{\mr{ऊ}}, the \textbf{independent long \emph{ū}}, used here because a Marathi word cannot stack one vowel mark on top of another — after \textbf{\mr{आ}}'s \textbf{\mr{ा}}, the second vowel needs its own full letter. \textbf{\mr{भ}} you have from \emph{bheṭū}. \emph{Bhā-ū}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{भाऊ}} is a \textbf{tadbhava} — not borrowed whole like \textbf{\mr{मित्र}} or \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}}, but the ordinary Prakrit-worn descendant of Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{भ्रातृ}} \emph{bhrātṛ}, three syllables ground down to two over a thousand years of speech. That root is Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*b\textsuperscript{h}réh\textsubscript{2}tēr}}, and here the family resemblance to English is not a false friend — it is the real thing: \textbf{brother}, Latin \textbf{frāter}, and Sanskrit's own \textbf{bhrātṛ} are all the same word, worn down four different ways by four different languages.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{bhāū} — brother
  \item \emph{Name:} three languages that share this root — English, Latin, Sanskrit
  \item \emph{Say it:} the three so far — \textbf{mitra, kuṭumb, bhāū}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\mr{भाऊ}} a tatsama or a tadbhava? (\textbf{Tadbhava} — worn down by sound change, not borrowed whole.) Which English word is the very same word as \textbf{\mr{भाऊ}}? (\textbf{Brother}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AD\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%8A}{Wiktionary: \mr{भाऊ}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bahīṇ]{\mr{बहीण} (bahīṇ) — sister, deliberately not English's cousin}

\label{lesson:MR-C11-bahin}



\begin{quote}
Three words so far: \textbf{mitra}, \textbf{kuṭumb}, \textbf{bhāū}. Say them, and say which one is a genuine cousin of an English word. (\textbf{Bhāū} — brother.) Its pair is not so simple.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{बहीण}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{बहीण}} — \emph{bahīṇ} — \textbf{sister} (feminine)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Nothing new. \textbf{\mr{ब}} from \emph{baraṃ}, \textbf{\mr{ह}} from \emph{namaskār}, \textbf{\mr{ी}} the familiar long \emph{ī}, \textbf{\mr{ण}} from every \textbf{-\mr{णे}} verb. \emph{Ba-hī-ṇ}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{बहीण}} is a \textbf{tadbhava}, worn down like \textbf{\mr{भाऊ}}: Old Marathi \emph{bahiṇī}, from Maharastri Prakrit \emph{bhaiṇī}, from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{भगिनी}} \emph{bhaginī}. There the resemblance to \textbf{brother}'s pair ends. \textbf{Bhaginī} is traditionally connected to \textbf{\mr{भज्}} \emph{bhaj-}, \textquotedblleft{}to share, to apportion\textquotedblright{} — a sister as one who shares in the household. That root has nothing to do with Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*swésōr}}, the ancestor of English \textbf{sister}. Two words that translate each other perfectly are, underneath, unrelated.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the chapter's whole shape, in two pairs}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{kind} & \textbf{route} \\
\midrule
\mr{मित्र}, \mr{कुटुंब} (\emph{mitra, kuṭumb}) & tatsama & taken up whole from Sanskrit \\
\mr{भाऊ}, \mr{बहीण} (\emph{bhāū, bahīṇ}) & tadbhava & worn down by Prakrit sound change \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Notice, too, how each pair \emph{looks}: \textbf{\mr{मित्र}} and \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}} carry conjuncts and marks a learner has to stop for; \textbf{\mr{भाऊ}} and \textbf{\mr{बहीण}} do not — plain consonants and vowels, the shape sound change tends to leave behind. And of the tadbhava pair, only \textbf{\mr{भाऊ}} is a secure English cousin; \textbf{\mr{बहीण}} is not.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} all four — \textbf{mitra, kuṭumb, bhāū, bahīṇ}
  \item \emph{Sort:} which two are tatsama, which two are tadbhava
  \item \emph{Name:} which sibling word is English's real cousin, and which is not — \textbf{bhāū} yes, \textbf{bahīṇ} no
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\mr{बहीण}} related to English \textbf{sister}? (\textbf{No} — a different Sanskrit root entirely.) Which sibling word \emph{is} related to its English counterpart? (\textbf{\mr{भाऊ}}, to \textbf{brother}.) Sort the chapter's four words into tatsama and tadbhava. (\textbf{Mitra, kuṭumb} — tatsama; \textbf{bhāū, bahīṇ} — tadbhava.) What did \textbf{\mr{कुटुंब}}'s gender turn out to be, against Hindi's? (\textbf{Neuter} here, masculine there.) And what did \textbf{\mr{मित्र}}'s root mean before \textquotedblleft{}friend\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{To bind}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AC\%E0\%A4\%B9\%E0\%A5\%80\%E0\%A4\%A3}{Wiktionary: \mr{बहीण}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AD\%E0\%A4\%97\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%A8\%E0\%A5\%80}{Wiktionary: \mr{भगिनी}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
